speakeroldname: Hon. R. O. Campney (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: MR. CAMPNEY    RELEASE TO PRESS OF CHANGES IN NATIONAL DEFENCE DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. Yesterday in my absence the hon. Leader of the Opposition complained to the Prime Minister about an unnamed' official of my department who, he alleged, had issued a statement to the press with respect to a matter about which he, the Leader of the Opposition, was deeply concerned. I have the relevant quotations here, which I should like to read. He referred on page 4749 of Hansard to "a statement issued yesterday by an official of the Department of National Defence", and again, dealing with certain material that appeared in the press, he said, "This was issued in the form of a statement handed to the press".
Later, on page 4750 of Hansard, he said referring again to certain material appearing in the press:
I understand that it is not in nearly as complete detail as the statement which was actually handed out.
Then he concludes on page 4750 of Hansard by asking a question as to "who the official is that issued this statement to the press and under whose authority".
First I should like to assure him that I did not either authorize or issue any such statement. I have consistently remained silent about the matter he has been discussing almost every day, until the department's estimates are being dealt with, when I understand he wants to raise the matter. I have made inquiries of each of my responsible officials, and each of them assures me that no such statement was issued, no such statement was authorized, and no such statement was prepared or even contemplated.

speakeroldname: Hon. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: MR. CAMPNEY    RELEASE TO PRESS OF CHANGES IN NATIONAL DEFENCE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this matter cannot be brushed off by a casual and evasive statement of this kind.

subtopic: MR. CAMPNEY    RELEASE TO PRESS OF CHANGES IN NATIONAL DEFENCE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: Oh!

subtopic: MR. CAMPNEY    RELEASE TO PRESS OF CHANGES IN NATIONAL DEFENCE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: What does the hon. member think is casual or evasive about it?

subtopic: MR. CAMPNEY    RELEASE TO PRESS OF CHANGES IN NATIONAL DEFENCE DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
It was very evasive because an attempt was made to create the impression
that this was not a statement. It was a statement, and whether it was verbal or written is unimportant. I think the minister is well aware that the Canadian Press did reproduce parts of that statement in direct quotes.

subtopic: MR. CAMPNEY    RELEASE TO PRESS OF CHANGES IN NATIONAL DEFENCE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, may I ask this question? Am I not to have my word accepted by the Leader of the Opposition?

subtopic: MR. CAMPNEY    RELEASE TO PRESS OF CHANGES IN NATIONAL DEFENCE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: Surely we have not yet reached the time when it is not possible to make any comment on a statement.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. CAMPNEY    RELEASE TO PRESS OF CHANGES IN NATIONAL DEFENCE DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
Perhaps we might all consider whether, whenever matters of this kind are to be raised, it would not be preferable that they be raised at the proper time and that we do not use the vehicle of questions of privilege, because by so doing a difficulty is created. There is nothing before the chair. A great deal of what is being said is a matter for argument, and that is something that should be debated at the proper time.
The minister has felt that he was justified in stating his position because he was not in the house yesterday when the matter was raised. To say that the statement of the minister is an evasive one is perhaps an expression which is too strong. The statement of the minister must be accepted as it is given, and no motives should be imputed. He has made a statement and it should be accepted. If any further arguments are to be made as to whether or not it was a statement, whether it was in one form or another, I think we fall into the realm of debate. At this moment, when there is nothing before the chair, I do not think we should carry on a debate under the pretext of a question of privilege. If there is to be a debate at this moment with respect to this matter, it would not be fair on the part of the chair to allow just the Leader of the Opposition and the minister to take part in this particular affair and not to let other members do so. I think we ought to reserve any argument on this point until the proper opportunity is afforded so that everybody can take part in the debate.

subtopic: MR. CAMPNEY    RELEASE TO PRESS OF CHANGES IN NATIONAL DEFENCE DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in what Your Honour has just said I submit that there is more than a question arising out of the discussion which has taken place between the minister and myself. Every day, or nearly

National Defence-Appointments every day, statements are made by ministers on a question of privilege, and the house has come to accept this practice and welcomes it.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. CAMPNEY    RELEASE TO PRESS OF CHANGES IN NATIONAL DEFENCE DEPARTMENT
speechtext:
May I interrupt the Leader of the Opposition just at the moment when he says that ministers every day make statements on questions of privilege. This is not so. I know the understanding of the Leader of the Opposition with respect to these statements, and with all due deference may I say that his understanding of the situation is not the right one. He is under the impression that ministers make statements by unanimous consent. They do it by practice, and that practice has been established for so long that today it may be regarded as a right.
I remember the argument raised by the Leader of the Opposition with respect to this point when he contended that he should have the right to comment on these statements. He claimed at the time that these statements made by ministers were being made by unanimous consent. But this is not so. If he wishes me to do so, I will deal with the matter on another occasion. I have not my notes with me at the moment. I have studied the matter carefully and I have a prepared statement which would elucidate the point satisfactorily. Let us therefore take this point as being one on which we all understand each other. When ministers rise to make statements on the orders of the day, on the calling of motions under routine proceedings, they do not do so by way of a question of privilege. They do so because it is a very old practice for ministers to make these statements, and they do it now as a matter of right.

subtopic: MR. CAMPNEY    RELEASE TO PRESS OF CHANGES IN NATIONAL DEFENCE DEPARTMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, since this matter has been raised and since these statements do become a matter of record, I would point out that the practice to which Your Honour has referred is an old practice which was followed at Westminster before there was a Canadian parliament and in our parliament ever since. If it were not so, then any statement could be made without challenge. I simply point out that in reporting a statement of this kind the Canadian Press-

subtopic: AGREEMENTS PROVIDING FOR CO-OPERATION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Secretary of Slate for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: AGREEMENTS PROVIDING FOR CO-OPERATION BETWEEN CANADA AND UNITED STATES
speechtext:
I should like to make a short announcement about two agreements concerning atomic energy which have been

signed this morning in Washington between the Canadian and United States governments. The first of these agreements provides for co-operation in the civil uses of atomic energy. The second agreement provides for co-operation regarding atomic information for mutual defence purposes.
Collaboration between Canada and the United States in atomic energy matters has, of course, been in effect since the commencement of the research and development programs in the two countries during the second world war. The revision of the United States atomic energy act in 1954 has made it possible to extend substantially the areas of such co-operation, and the two agreements to which I have just referred are designed to take advantage of this fact. I am confident that the co-operation made possible by these agreements will be to the mutual advantage of both the United States and Canada, and that this extension of our long-standing partnership will make a material contribution to the application of atomic energy both for constructive purposes, and for the protection of the free world.
The texts of the agreements will be made public in Canada by tabling in parliament within a day or two, on a date to be mutually agreed upon by the two governments.

subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO ADVERTISE- MENT IN MONTREAL "GAZETTE"
speechtext:
On Monday the hon.
member for Burnaby-Coquitlam referred to an advertisement in the Montreal Gazette by the Czech legation about an amnesty proclaimed in Czechoslovakia. The Czech legation is free, following normal advertising practice, to distribute information about the terms of this amnesty by means of a press release or by advertisement in a newspaper. In this case it was done without the knowledge or of course without the approval of the Canadian government. As I mentioned at that time, Mr. Speaker, in my preliminary reply to this question, the advertisement is addressed to Czechoslovak citizens and therefore cannot, as such, be considered officially as improper as it would undoubtedly be if it were addressed or directed to Canadian citizens of Czechoslovak origin or former nationality.
I am sure, Mr. Speaker, that any Czechs or Slovaks in Canada who have escaped from Czechoslovakia since the communist coup in 1948, and who may see this advertisement, will not be misled by it and will examine carefully what this amnesty does and does not promise before deciding to return. There is no amnesty at all for political prisoners and the amnesty afforded to those who merely left the country illegally is both limited and ambiguously worded. Furthermore, anybody who returned to Czechoslovakia on the strength of this amnesty and did not like what he found out there about its application would doubtless find it very difficult-to say the least-to leave again.

Mr. Chairman, there is a reason why the minister should make a statement, and that is that members of the house generally were not present at the meetings of the committee. It is not suggested that


at any time discussions before a committee answer the need for explanation in the house.
I would point out that at the time this bill was before the house on an earlier occasion there were certain clauses that had very important applications, in the minds of some hon. members. Those were discussed in committee. I am well aware, from reports that have come from that committee, that there was one clause in particular in regard to which the minister gave a very clear and explicit undertaking. I am referring to clause 27.
It has been customary, at the time when a bill first comes before the committee where amendments are being made that are in response to earlier discussion, to explain what amendments the minister proposes to deal with, so that there may be a discussion, not merely for the purpose of extending debate at the outset but for the purpose of making it possible to consider any alternative amendments that might be desirable when that section is actually called.
For that reason I would have hoped that, at least in regard to clause 27, the minister would have indicated what he is prepared to do, and why, in view of the explicit undertaking he gave when the matter was under discussion on second reading, he had decided to limit the amendments to those now included in our copies of the bill. I should like to be sure first that the amendment he proposes to make in this house sitting as a committee of the whole is in accordance with the inserts that we have. And second, why he is only prepared to go that far in making an amendment. I would point out that this has been the practice, and that there have been many occasions when ministers, upon the discussion at this stage, have become convinced that it would be desirable to follow another course and have been advised on drafting an alternative amendment, and that has saved time when we reached the appropriate section.

subtopic: CONSOLIDATION OF LEGISLATION-AUTHORIZATION FOR OPERATION OF TELECOMMUNICATION SYSTEM, ETC.
speechtext:
Because in my earlier parliamentary experience I have found it necessary to confine myself to the section under consideration, I hesitated to talk on clause 1 about matters which concern later clauses of the bill.
There was certainly no intention on my part not to follow the traditional practice of the house. I had thought, Mr. Chairman, that when we came to clause 18 I might then suggest that the committee should consider at that time both clauses 18 and 27, which refer to the question just raised by the Leader of the Opposition. If the Leader of the Opposition feels it would contribute to the discussion if I were to make some statement concerning these two clauses now I would be very happy to accommodate him; but really, Mr. Chairman, I had thought that a more appropriate time would be when we reach clause 18.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would refer particularly to a discussion which took place as reported at page 4076 of Hansard of May 24. This will explain why I should think it would be appropriate if the minister would indicate why the amendment to clause 27 that is being proposed is in fact being proposed at this time. As reported at page 4076 of Hansard, I said this to the minister:
The minister has said "it is intended". I would point out that it is not a matter of what is intended: it is what the act says. I have asked a fair question. Does the minister propose to introduce an amendment which will specifically declare that the Canadian National Railway Company in operating such services as are covered by section 27 will be subject to provincial regulations, licensing and toll rates?
The answer of the minister, as reported at page 4077, was as follows:
Mr. Speaker, I thought it was already perfectly clear from what I have said, but if the Leader of the Opposition does not feel my answer was sufficiently categorical I wish to say it is my intention definitely to propose an amendment in that sense. I hope the Leader of the Opposition is satisfied that this is the kind of categorical answer he would like to have.
In spite of that categorical statement, Mr. Chairman, the amendment contains no such provision. I should think, therefore, that at this point the minister might well explain to us why he has withdrawn from that position and why the amendment, which falls far short of that, is in fact to be given consideration.

subtopic: CONSOLIDATION OF LEGISLATION-AUTHORIZATION FOR OPERATION OF TELECOMMUNICATION SYSTEM, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is just
because I made that very categorical statement in reply to the Leader of the Opposition that I have given a great deal of attention to carrying out the undertaking which I gave to the house. While the Leader of the Opposition may not agree that that undertaking is being discharged, because after all I fully realize that legal texts do sometimes lend themselves to discussion, and sometimes lend themselves to more interpretations than one, I am firmly convinced, Mr. Chairman, that the two amendments-the hon. Leader of the Opposition has referred to only one-referring specifically to clauses 18 and 27 have the effect of carrying out in every detail the undertaking, if I may call it that, 50433-304J
Canadian National Railways that I gave to the house on May 24 when the bill was discussed. I still feel, after this preliminary exchange of comments with regard to the matter, that the subject can best, be discussed when we come to clause 18. Perhaps, if it is then agreeable to the committee, clauses 18 and 27 could be considered at that time because of the very close link between them.

subtopic: CONSOLIDATION OF LEGISLATION-AUTHORIZATION FOR OPERATION OF TELECOMMUNICATION SYSTEM, ETC.
speechtext:
No, Mr. Chairman. Following the long-established practice that on the first item it is appropriate to indicate suggested changes that should be considered by the government for possible further amendments,. I propose to indicate that the government, should now give consideration to the further-amendment, certainly of clause 27, and possibly clause 18 to such extent as may be necessary to make it conform with clause 27. I do that because, if the minister accepted the arguments that we make, he could then give the appropriate instructions for the drafting, and when we come to those clauses we would be ready to deal with them and save the amount of time that would otherwise be involved.
In the discussion that took place at the time that this act was before us, it was pointed out that there was a general desire on the-part of those who spoke in regard to clause 27 and also clause 18 that the Canadian National Railways should have such authority and such powers as were desirable for the operation as; a railway so that we may at the very outset anticipate any possible suggestion that there was any opposition to the general purposes of this act in so far as consolidation of the existing legislation is concerned. I should like to say now that we strongly favour the consolidation of this act, and by that consolidation the simplification of a number of statutory provisions affecting the Canadian. National Railways.
We have pointed out, however, why clause-27, with the influence upon it of clause 18,. should not stand in its present form and, in fact, why it is not necessary at all. Just to indicate some of the difficulties that we have in regard to some of these matters I would point out that, when I read the powers conferred upon the operating transport company of the Canadian National Railways, that is Canadian National Transportation, Limited, one of the explanations given was that it was desirable to have these general powers so that the name of the Canadian National Railways could be on the trucks and. other motor vehicles they were operating:. I would point out that we do not need any-amendment to this act for that purpose. As a matter of curiosity, I walked down to the station and to the freight area behind, and I

Canadian National Railways find that, under the act as it now stands, vehicles operated by the transportation company of the Canadian National Railways have on them "Canadian National Railways" and not "Canadian National Transportation, Limited". Therefore there is no need to include this amendment for any purpose of that kind.
Having regard to the extremely wide powers conferred upon Canadian National Transportation, Limited, which is the company now operating trucks and buses and other motor vehicles, and having regard to the fact that those powers are similar to the powers exercised by the Canadian Pacific Railway under its corresponding act, I submit that we have not had placed before us a single reason of any kind why clause 27 should be included in this act. As against that, there has been the representation of competent lawyers before the committee expressing the opinion that the inclusion of clause 27 takes the operation of truck and bus services by the Canadian National Railways outside of the jurisdiction of the provincial governments.
Mr. Chairman, again so that there may be no confusion in the argument, we are not called upon to debate here the question of the wisdom of placing transportation of this kind under provincial jurisdiction. It was the federal government which made that decision last year and came before us to seek the support of this house for the Motor Vehicle Transport Act. It will be recalled that after the privy council, following long years of litigation, had declared that interprovincial transportation of this kind was under the authority of the federal government, for reasons which may be best known to themselves the federal government decided not to exercise that power conferred upon them by the legal interpretation of our constitution but asked the provinces to take over the supervision and control of motor vehicle transportation.

subtopic: CONSOLIDATION OF LEGISLATION-AUTHORIZATION FOR OPERATION OF TELECOMMUNICATION SYSTEM, ETC.
speechtext: Authorized them to take it over.

subtopic: CONSOLIDATION OF LEGISLATION-AUTHORIZATION FOR OPERATION OF TELECOMMUNICATION SYSTEM, ETC.
speechtext:
They invited them to take it over. They did not just passively authorize them to take it over. The privy council, following extended arguments by the federal government, had given a decision that the federal government had authority over this type of transport. Instead of exercising that authority conferred upon them by the judgment after long years of litigation, the federal government then invited the provincial representatives to come here to Ottawa, proposed to them that they should take over this supervision and indicated that for the purpose of placing transportation of this kind under the

provincial authorities a Motor Vehicle Transport Act would be passed by this parliament, so that the effect of the privy council decision which this government had sought would be overcome by such legislation. The provincial governments, which had been fighting in the courts for that right, very naturally accepted the proposal of the federal government.
Therefore we are not dealing with the wisdom or otherwise at this stage of that decision. That was the decision of this government. They fought for the right to control it, and then, having got the right they asked the provinces to take it over. We as members of parliament were asked to support legislation which would implement that proposal. That legislation is now on the books. Until such time as this government comes back to the house and says, "That was a mistake; we should have exercised our powers under the privy council judgment and we should control transportation of this kind", then we as a parliament are bound to respect the position taken in relation to the provinces when this was under discussion last year.
With regard to the clause now before us, clause 27, in its legal effect, I concede that there are always possible arguments about the interpretation of statutes. Nevertheless I do submit, and in making that submission I am supported by a number of arguments that have been made outside this house by lawyers with wide constitutional experience, that the effect of clause 27 is to take the operation of motor vehicles by the Canadian National Railways outside of the authority of the provincial governments and thus create the very kind of confusion which the Motor Vehicle Transport Act intended to remove. This clause will create confusion as to what authority there is over motor vehicle transport.
If the Canadian National Railways can operate buses and trucks outside of provincial authority then most certainly those operating the same type of vehicles will seek the same right and will feel a sense of injustice if they do not have that right because of the position taken by this government last year.
Last year before they called the provinces here and made the proposal to them, they would have had a perfect right to say that the privy council has conferred the responsibility upon them and not only the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway but every other interprovincial bus operation or truck operation is going to be under federal authority. They decided, however, against that. They placed the control under the provinces. They will create endless confusion if by the effect of section 27 they give to one truck operation or one bus operation a right with regard to interprovincial

operation which is not conferred by statute and in fact is denied by statute to other similar operations.

subtopic: CONSOLIDATION OF LEGISLATION-AUTHORIZATION FOR OPERATION OF TELECOMMUNICATION SYSTEM, ETC.
speechtext: Does my hon. friend mean "intra" or "inter"?

subtopic: CONSOLIDATION OF LEGISLATION-AUTHORIZATION FOR OPERATION OF TELECOMMUNICATION SYSTEM, ETC.
speechtext: I mean "inter"; if I used the word "intraprovincial" I had intended at that point to use the word "interprovincial". I shall come to the use of the word "intraprovincial" because the fact is that the cases make it quite clear that under section 27 even intraprovincial operation of buses and trucks by the Canadian National Railways would not be under provincial authority. That is something that should be borne in mind by the hon. members who were called upon last year to support the Motor Vehicle Transport Act at the request of this government following the conference with the provincial representatives. I know this argument has already been placed before the government but nevertheless I think hon. members should know-and particularly those members who were not on the committee-that there have been decisions that transportation entirely within the bounds of a province is outside of provincial authority if it is part of a national transportation system. A case already referred to is the case of Luscar Collieries v. McDonald, (1927) Appeal Cases, at page 925.

subtopic: CONSOLIDATION OF LEGISLATION-AUTHORIZATION FOR OPERATION OF TELECOMMUNICATION SYSTEM, ETC.
speechtext: That was the case of a rail line.

subtopic: CONSOLIDATION OF LEGISLATION-AUTHORIZATION FOR OPERATION OF TELECOMMUNICATION SYSTEM, ETC.
speechtext:
Of course it was the case of a rail line. But the question of transportation makes no difference. If this is brought under the operation of the Canadian National Railways by section 27, it is all transportation and, being transportation, will be under the general application of the law to the Canadian National Railways. I ask not only those trained in the law but those who can read the statutes-and every hon. member can read them easily-to recognize that it is not just rail lines; it is the transportation system afforded by the Canadian National Railways that is outside of the authority of provincial governments if this authority is granted.
I would point out that in the case of Luscar Collieries v. McDonald, to which I have already referred, it was a rail line that was under consideration. It was operated wholly within the boundaries of Alberta. There is the clear and express intention of parliament that they should not be considered works for the general advantage of Canada and they are expressly excluded by the third subsection of clause 18.
I come back to the argument that, because of the provisions of section 92, subsection 10, of the British North America Act, which gives to the provinces jurisdiction over local works

Canadian National Railways and undertakings, to the extent the operations carried out under clause 27 are wholly intraprovincial, wholly carried out within the limits of the province, they fall definitely under the jurisdiction of the province so far as they are carried out within the province.
Then, Mr. Chairman, the question comes up, what about operations which are carried out interprovincially, between a point in one province and a point in another province? It seems to me on that point the matter is also equally clear. There is the Motor Vehicle Transport Act, and after reading its terms I cannot see how they can fail to apply to operations carried out under the authority of clause 27. It seems to me that an operation carried out by Canadian National Railways between one province and another is clearly an interprovincial undertaking, and is clearly the kind of undertaking which parliament said at the last session would he subject to the terms of the Motor Vehicle Transport Act. It seems to me, therefore, that we come down to this. If the operations carried out by the railway under clause 27 are carried out within a province, then those operations are provincial and are within the meaning of section 92, subsection 10, of the British North America Act and are within the legislative jurisdiction of the province in which they are carried out. To the extent that they are not intraprovincial but on the contrary interprovincial, then I believe they are fully covered under the provisions of the Motor Vehicle Transport Act, of which the Leader of the Opposition spoke this morning. As hon. members will recall, that act enables the governments of those provinces which wish to have the act proclaimed to exercise over interprovincial motor traffic the same kind of authority as they exercise over intraprovincial traffic.
As I said before the committee, I approached the question of the drafting of clauses 18 and 27 with a great deal of interest, particularly in view of the categoric statement I had made in answer to a question by the Leader of the Opposition. I would like to have found some simple language which would, in effect, have reproduced in this statute what I said to the Leader of the Opposition, namely that the operations under clause 27 would be subject to the jurisdiction of the province or something along those lines. But when I came to consider the difficulties that gave rise to, not only with respect to clause 27, but with respect to other clauses of the bill, it seemed to me that that simple though direct method of amendment to the sections in question would have to be rejected. I believe if you stop to consider clause 27 for a moment you will realize that,

whatever operations are carried out under that section, they will be subject to a number of laws.
Surely, we have to admit that the drivers of the trucks operating under clause 27 are going to be subject to the provisions of the Criminal Code. Surely, we are going to have to admit that the operators of these trucks likewise must respect municipal bylaws concerning parking and speed on city streets. Surely, we must also recognize that they must respect provincial legislation with regard to speed on the highways and the paying of licences. It seemed to me when I came to consider clause 27 that there were operations which were going to be subject to laws at all levels of government, federal, provincial and municipal. If one singled out clause 27 as being the place where one said expressly that the powers granted Canadian National Railways under that clause were to be carried out subject to the rights or jurisdiction of the provinces, surely there was immediately an implication that applied to a large number of the other clauses of the bill and that they likewise would have to be exercised subject to the jurisdiction of the provinces.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, after considering that difficulty it seemed to me that we would have to come back to rely on two important points. First of all we would have to rely on the fact that clause 27 of the bill makes it abundantly clear that what we are giving the Canadian National Railways is not a right in the sense of a franchise but we are giving them a corporate power to do certain things, namely to buy, sell, lease or operate motor vehicles of all kinds for the carriage of traffic. There is a restriction, however, that it must be in conjunction with or in substitution for rail service under their management and control.
Second, Mr. Chairman, we must surely attach some importance to the express exclusion in clause 18 of what is done under clause 27 as being a work for the general advantage of Canada. Is there a lawyer in the committee who believes that the mere fact of the attachment-if I may use that expression-to the national system of some small bus line replacing a railway line that has been abandoned by the railway is going to be held by the courts to be a work for the general advantage of Canada in the face of the express exclusion contained in clause 18? Surely, Mr. Chairman, that is straining the normal use of the English language to the breaking point.
Mr. Chairman, I am sorry I have taken so long in replying to the Leader of the Opposition; but it does seem to me that with

It is essential that the country should have the free and unhampered use of the cheapest forms of transport and therefore no restrictions which would unfairly prejudice the road user should be imposed. The railways themselves should be empowered to provide and operate services of road vehicles, subject to whatever restrictions are imposed upon other road transport operators. On the other hand, in our opinion, in Canada, where of necessity freight must be conveyed in large quantities over long distances at all times of the year, railway transportation is essential to the economic welfare of the country. Because they are essential and because the railway freight rate structure implies conditions approximating to a quasi-monopoly, the railways require, if they are to continue to operate efficiently, a measure of protection from long distance road competition and an equalization of the conditions under which short distance traffic is carried.

In recent years the Canadian National Railways, which has this line into Prince Rupert and also a line running into Vancouver, had this boat service connecting the two railway lines. I point out that many, many years ago the Grand Trunk Railway Company was given the power to operate shipping lines. I refer to chapter 58 of the statutes of 1888, section 12, which reads as follows:
The company may own or hire and run steamships for carrying freight and passengers to and from any port with which their lines of railway connect, to and from any port in Great Britain or Ireland.
Obviously it made sense for the Grand Trunk to operate a ship service connecting their railway terminals. In effect that is what has been done on the west coast for many years.
In my time Prince Rupert has always been regarded as a Canadian National port. This company has had a regular boat service and very fine C.N.R. crews experienced on that coast for all these years. It is a very difficult coast. There are no finer seamen on it than the men who have been working for the C.N.R. As hon. members know, in recent years that part of British Columbia has been opening up very rapidly. There is the aluminum smelter at Kitimat where eventually there is to be a city of 25,000 or 30,000 people. Prince Rupert itself has been going ahead

very rapidly. There is to be a huge smelter farther up the coast on the Taku river, established by the Frobisher people. There is also talk of huge power developments on the Stikine river. The whole of that part of Canada is opening up. This was certainly considered, though not exclusively, as Canadian National territory.
Just when this part of the country is developing, the Canadian National goes out of the regular steamship service and makes an agreement with the Canadian Pacific under which the C.P.R. ship is to be regularly used in service, and the C.N.R. will only have a ship for cruises in the summer. The result has been that men who held very responsible posts on C.N.R. ships have been either reduced to lower positions at great financial sacrifice, or else many of the men in the crews have lost their jobs entirely.

Some years ago I said we had the building of a new ship under consideration and indeed in the 1952 and 1953 budget we had an estimate for the building of a ship, which was approved.

Yes; I should be pleased to make a brief statement.
The purpose of this bill-and the only purpose-is to carry out the recommendation of the joint committee of both houses on the library which was adopted unanimously in this house on June 23, 1954, and which appears in the Votes and Proceedings of that date. The second part of the report reads as follows:
That at the next session of parliament, the Library of Parliament Act be amended so as to have only one librarian in charge of the whole library from such time as one of the present joint librarians may retire; it being understood that there shall be an associate librarian who shall be required to possess the full and practical knowledge of the official language which is not that of the librarian for the time being, and that the librarian should be alternately English speaking and French speaking according to the unwritten rule which has always been observed for the speakership and elsewhere.
The bill does not, in fact, make any provision about the mother tongue or the language of the persons who shall occupy these positions. On searching the statutes it was found that this had never been done, and it was felt that the same unwritten conventions that govern Your Honour's position here in this house were conventions that any government of any complexion could be relied upon to carry out in the implementation of this bill.
Of course, like any other measure having to do with parliament this one is in form -but not in any other way-a government measure. It is the result of the work of the joint committee on the library in which I think there is no politics whatsoever. During the time I have been associated with that committee since I became a member of parliament-and that is not very long ago, I admit

Library of Parliament Act -I have found that all the members of the committee co-operate in the interests of giving the best possible service to members of parliament.
The fundamental reason for this departure at this time is that it was felt that it would be more efficient to have one person responsible for the administration of the library rather than two. There was an additional reason which was in the mind, I think, of some of the members of the committee, and it was this. In 1885, at the time provision was made for two librarians instead of one, Sir John Macdonald, who introduced the amendment, gave these as his reasons. If the house would bear with me for a moment or two I should like to read what he said on May 6, 1885:
The object of the resolution is to alter, in some degree, the constitution, and increase the staff of the library. Instead of having one librarian, as before, it is proposed that there shall be two officers, who shall hold a joint commission, one to be known as the general librarian and the other as the parliamentary librarian ... A parliamentary library proper is a library that contains all the works necessary for the use of members of parliament. But here, as in Washington, we have no British museum, no general library, considered as a national one, but under the name of a parliamentary library we have increased the number of books so much as to make it become a national one. It has grown so vast that we think it ought to assume that position in every respect. In order to carry out that project, if it is satisfactory to the house, it is proposed that there shall be two librarians, holding a joint commission, one to be known as the general librarian, whose special duties will be to look after the library as a whole, as a scientific and literary institution, and the other to be a parliamentary librarian, the object being that he shall apply himself specially to parliamentary precedents, and see that the latest and best works connected with constitutional law and history and political subjects generally are obtained.
It was not very many years ago that parliament established a national library, which is now set up to serve one of the two purposes that Sir John Macdonald said the library of parliament was serving in 1885. The special functions attributed at that time to the general librarian are now performed by the national librarian and in that sense, of course, the position of general librarian has become redundant.
It will be noted, of course, that it is not intended to disturb either of the present incumbents, and that the bill will only go into effect upon the retirement-and perhaps I should say "or demise", which we hope will not precede their retirement-of one or other of the librarians.

In the past there have been two librarians heading the library of parliament and, as we all know, their qualifications have been long years of experience. Certainly no one questions their ability, but when the time comes for their retirement what is going to happen? I imagine also that retirement is not far distant. The government gives no indication and no assurance that it will appoint a qualified person to head such a large and expensive show piece of parliament, as well as a useful part of it. While academic and professional standards are being raised everywhere, the government pays no attention to this.
One of the finest libraries in Canada could become something of a political plum without a guarantee from the government that scholarship and not political patronage will dictate the appointment of future parliamentary librarians. I believe it is an insult to trained librarians and to the Canadian library association. On more than one occasion the library association has passed resolutions urging that no person should be appointed to libraries anywhere in Canada who is not properly qualified. At the annual meeting of the Canadian library association in 1953 the following resolution was passed:
Be it resolved that this association urge upon the government of Canada that library appointments in all departments and agencies of government be made under the provisions of the Civil Service Act in respect to professional qualifications and merit.
In the bill the government ignores that resolution. In public libraries throughout Ontario standards are very zealously guarded. Trained librarians must have a bachelor of arts degree and a bachelor of library science degree. These are the minimum qualifications for a librarian. Many students go on to get their master of arts and their master of library science degrees. These young people go to these schools at their own expense and are trained for these jobs. I have been told by the Canadian library association that there are two library schools in Canada accredited by the American library association. These are the library schools of the universities of McGill and Toronto.

Entrance qualifications to both library schools are a bachelor of arts degree from a recognized university and a reading knowledge of both English and French. The degree given by both McGill and Toronto is that of library science. The B.A. plus the B.L.S. are now required for professional positions in Canadian libraries. Unless the government changes its mind, it can take inexperienced persons and train them at the expense of the taxpayers. One library of parliament official claims that long experience in the library of parliament is training as good as or even better than graduation from a library school. This point of view is open to argument, but the fact remains it is unfair to librarians and unfair to the taxpayers to provide that experience at public expense.

library science or master of library science from schools recognized by the Canadian library association. In the Toronto public libraries, and I mention them because they are within my own ken, scholarship is of the utmost importance. This is also true of the national library in Ottawa. This suggestion was never mentioned at any of the meetings of the committee, and it is not unfair to say that the whole idea came from outside the house after the committee reported. But before I come to deal with that, which is the most serious point, raised by the hon. member for York-Humber (Miss Aitken) and supported by nearly everybody else who spoke, I Should like to say something about the other points raised.
The hon. member for Macleod talked about the necessity for having more help for members of parliament to criticize the government. I think they need more help. I certainly agree with him. I suppose the hon. member for Macleod was thinking of providing help to the opposition on the lavish scale on which it is provided in the legislature of his province.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO IMPLEMENT RECOMMENDATIONS OF JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext: What does that mean?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO IMPLEMENT RECOMMENDATIONS OF JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight), raised a further question about the language of the librarian and the associate librarian under the new legislation. I think I should repeat here that the government felt there ought not to be in the bill itself a departure in this respect for the first time, as far as we were able to discover, in legislation since confederation. We felt that, regardless of what party or group of parties might form a government at any time, that convention would be respected. It is perfectly obvious that if we are to give equal opportunities to all members of the house, regardless of which of the official languages is their mother tongue, it is essential that one of the senior officers in the library be a person to whom any member can talk in his mother tongue. I do not believe there is any dissent from that anywhere in the house.
It was suggested that there might be some danger, unless an amendment were made to this legislation, of the office of librarian becoming a political plum. Well, sir, I had a little research done for me on that point.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO IMPLEMENT RECOMMENDATIONS OF JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext: By whom?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO IMPLEMENT RECOMMENDATIONS OF JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext: The librarians.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO IMPLEMENT RECOMMENDATIONS OF JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I can let the hon. member make his own surmises. I find that in no case when this party has had charge of the government or occupied the treasury benches has anyone ever been appointed librarian except a member of the staff of the library. I find, however, that when the party of the hon. gentlemen opposite was in office and this position fell vacant, it was customary to appoint someone from outside the library staff, someone who had been prominently associated with their party.
Actually the real reason Sir John Macdonald brought in this silly legislation which we are now asking the house to repeal was that he had appointed a gentleman named Mr. Martin Griffin, who was a journalist in Toronto, to the job of librarian when it became vacant, and there was such an outcry from his supporters in another part of the country that he brought in this legislation to create two positions, so he could satisfy both claimants. A very distinguished member of Sir Robert Borden's government occupied the position of librarian for a good many years. He was still here when I first came to Ottawa, and in my opinion he discharged his functions very well indeed.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO IMPLEMENT RECOMMENDATIONS OF JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext: Was he a professional librarian?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO IMPLEMENT RECOMMENDATIONS OF JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext:
No, of course he was not; but he was a cultivated gentleman and a very good librarian. Now, I do not think there is any question that it would be preferable, other things being equal, to have as librarian a person trained in what is called library science. I was approached, as many other hon. members obviously were, by people who were interested, and I think perhaps I should read to the house now the reply I made on this point, because this will be the position I intend to take on the hon. lady's amendment and which I hope my friends in the house and the hon. member for Greenwood, who like me has a soft spot for the humanities, will find it possible to support. In this communication I said:
The bill ... is designed to carry out the recommendations of the joint committee on the library. I am afraid I would not be disposed to recommend, or even to support, an amendment such as that suggested by the Canadian library association. I agree that it is of great importance to have trained librarians on the library staff, and that, other things being equal, it would be desirable to have a trained librarian as head of the library.
But in this world other things are not always equal,-
As, I might say parenthetically, I discovered not so long ago.
-and there is a great variety of qualities required in a good parliamentary librarian, and I would think it most undesirable to have parliament restrict the freedom of choice of the governor in council in making on rare occasions when it
Library of Parliament Act
becomes necessary the most suitable selection, all things taken into account, from the whole Canadian population.
I go so far as to say, Mr. Speaker, that I do not think the fact of having been a distinguished member of the privy council- as Mr. Martin Burrell was-should be a necessary disqualification.
I was flattered, as I am sure were all my colleagues on the treasury benches, by the appeals from the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Hees) in particular and from several other hon. members that the government should give an assurance that the right kind of person would be appointed to this position. I have no hesitation in giving such an assurance so long as the Liberal party is on this side of the house. We hope these appointments will not have to be made for a considerable time, but if they are made I am quite sure that as long as the right hon. gentleman who is now Prime Minister occupies his present post, he would not make any recommendation except one which he thought would serve all hon. members on both sides of the house.
As I say, Mr. Speaker, desirable as it would be to have someone who was a trained library scientist, it seems to me there are other qualities that are even more important in the head of a library. Most important of all, it seems to me, is a good general education, with a strong bias toward history, constitutional law and political subjects.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO IMPLEMENT RECOMMENDATIONS OF JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext: And a liking for the Liberal party.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO IMPLEMENT RECOMMENDATIONS OF JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Like Mr. Burrell. It seems to me it is unlikely that anyone on either side of the house who happened to occupy the position now occupied by the present Prime Minister, with the responsibility given under this legislation or under the previous legislation, would make any appointment which was unworthy.
That leads me to make reference to the most recent of all appointments, namely that of the present librarian, who was recommended by the Prime Minister's predecessor, Mr. Mackenzie King. As all hon. members know, Mr. Hardy is not a trained librarian but he is a very cultivated man. I do not think anybody on either side of the house would say that Mr. Hardy was anything but completely impartial in the discharge of his duties.

We now have-as we did not have, I presume, years ago-a body of trained librarians. It is now a profession in a sense in which it was not so recognized not so many years ago.
I would hope that we can make the best of both worlds by getting not only a person with a good general education, as the minister has indicated, but also a person with special qualifications. Mr. Chairman, I think we support the amendment. I should like to reiterate what my colleague has said regarding the present library service. As far as the present librarians are concerned I think we will all say we have been very satisfied. Let me point out that these gentlemen are not concerned at all with the bill, because it will only come into effect after their retirement takes place.
May I say that I did not like the tone of the minister's speech. I think he interjected into this quite routine matter, a subject of some seriousness and importance, a political element which may have been engendered by the debates of the last few days but certainly is not justified thereby.
I want to make my attitude perfectly clear on another question. The minister mentioned what I said about language. I thought I had made it very clear that I was not prejudiced either for or against anybody on account of the language he happened to use.

Library of Parliament Act thing. speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a word in support of the amendment. I certainly do not agree with the hon. member for Macleod when he suggests that this might be a reflection, or might even be remotely construed as a reflection, upon the present incumbents in our library.

It is true that the senior members of the staff would not be qualified under the bill because at the time they received their appointment the degrees of bachelor and master of library science were virtually unknown. It is something that has been recognized as a necessity within the last two decades. Men such as the present chief librarian, men like Hon. Martin Burrell and others to whom the minister referred, certainly were efficient librarians, but if the present incumbent, for example, were being appointed today and made an application I am sure he would have a degree or he would not expect to receive the appointment. When he dealt with the bill in the first place he spoke very matter of factly. He was really simply the mouthpiece of the library of parliament committee, and that was all. It was only incidental that he was introducing the bill. He had no views and he could not do anything about it because

Library of Parliament Act this was the report of the library of parliament committee. But when the amendment was produced he said immediately that the government would not accept it. I have never seen a greater change in emphasis, standing first on one foot and then on the other, as the minister displayed after the hon. member for York-Humber introduced the amendment.
But regardless of the qualifications of the persons who hold these positions today, I am thinking of the young people of the country. I have known some of them who, at great expense and sacrifice, by borrowing money and everything else, have gone through university to obtain these degrees. Within the last 20 years they have developed in this country and elsewhere a profession of which they are proud. It was only a few centuries ago when even members of the medical profession were not too well qualified. After all, at one time in this country we had barbers as surgeons. However, I am quite sure that today no one, including the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, would suggest that even the best looking barber in Canada should be appointed to a medical staff anywhere. The same thing is true of the lawyers; they have evolved in the same way. The jewelers evolved from the old pawnbrokers. All throughout history we have this matter of evolution, and this is one sample of that evolution which has taken place, a professional evolution.
I would say, sir, it would be most unfortunate if we in the parliament of Canada, who are supposed to be setting an example, setting standards for our young people in this country, by our legislation set very low standards. True, this position was established first in 1885 and now it is being amended, but we should at least try to bring it into line with today's conditions. We should recognize the sacrifices these young people are making. We should recognize the qualifications of our library science schools. There is no municipal board anywhere in the country which has a municipal library which would not require, as a prerequisite to appointment as librarian, graduation from a library school. Are we going to adopt a lower standard? It is for that reason I am going to support this amendment.

In my opinion, Mr. Chairman, we need as chief librarian here a man who primarily has administrative ability. I do not suggest, nor does the bill suggest, that he could not also be a trained librarian. I do not think for one moment that we should restrict such an important position to only those who are trained as librarians.

speechtext: That is obvious, but I would not expect the minister to admit it.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO IMPLEMENT RECOMMENDATIONS OF JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext: I would like to ask the minister one question. I understand that under this bill a librarian is to be appointed, and then there will be authority for the appointment of an associate librarian. Does the minister feel that neither the librarian nor the associate should be a qualified librarian? He mentioned a minute ago that these others were still deputies in the different departments. The hon. member for Timiskaming mentioned the Minister of National Health and Welfare, and suggested that he had done an excellent job.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO IMPLEMENT RECOMMENDATIONS OF JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext: That is right.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO IMPLEMENT RECOMMENDATIONS OF JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext: That is all very fine; but do you think he could have done that job if he had not had a fully qualified man as his deputy?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO IMPLEMENT RECOMMENDATIONS OF JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext: Under him.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO IMPLEMENT RECOMMENDATIONS OF JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext: I am referring to Dr. Cameron. He is the man who has helped the Minister of National Health and Welfare do a good job, as the hon. member for Timiskaming has said. Does the minister feel that neither the librarian nor the associate should be a qualified person? Surely one of them at least should be qualified.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO IMPLEMENT RECOMMENDATIONS OF JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext: I think they should both be qualified.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO IMPLEMENT RECOMMENDATIONS OF JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext: Qualified librar-v ians?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO IMPLEMENT RECOMMENDATIONS OF JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext:
But I do not think the only or indeed the major qualification for a good head or associate head of a library is necessarily that he be a man with a library science degree. I think we would be making a great mistake in this house if we limited appointments to these two positions to such a comparatively small part of the whole

Canadian population, particularly when their salaries are being paid out of everybody's taxes.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO IMPLEMENT RECOMMENDATIONS OF JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, let us keep the discussion on a reasonable basis. The suggestion made in relation to the Minister of National Health and Welfare has no application whatever to this. A comparable suggestion would be to put a mining engineer in charge of a hospital, and you would not do that, of course.
So far as a medical position is concerned you would appoint a skilled medical practitioner. If it were a legal position you would appoint a lawyer. And as far as administrative posts are concerned in the ordinary course of events governments call upon men or women to administer departments without regard to technical qualifications. Even the Minister of Fisheries may learn something about fish after he has spent some years with that department. The fact that he might not have known a plaice from a haddock in the first instance does not mean that he could not do a good job, so long as the administrative task was well done. The comparison is not there.
A very serious attempt has been made in Canada in recent years to bring the position of librarian into the field of responsible professions. Everyone has agreed that this is an important task. In order to attract people to this profession it is necessary to give them the feeling that the training they get will be recognized. I have heard no suggestion made which would offer any reason why this amendment should not be accepted, having regard to the length of time which has already been devoted to the training of librarians in this country. Perhaps ten years ago, fifteen years ago, it could not have been done because this is a comparatively modern development. Now we have plenty of trained librarians.
Unless there is some reason that has not been indicated by the minister it would be a desirable thing to offer the encouragement that would be offered to those who have been training as librarians by making this profession a requirement under the act itself, and I am supporting the amendment on that ground.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO IMPLEMENT RECOMMENDATIONS OF JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I am quite surprised that the government is apparently refusing to grant professional status to the many graduate librarians throughout Canada. What the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration said a moment ago was, if you require that the persons who are given these jobs must have professional qualifications you will be limiting the field. That is precisely the situation 50433-307}
Library of Parliament Act that obtains in other professions. One would not think of filling a post that required a medical doctor unless the appointee was properly qualified. The same thing applies to members of the legal profession. I suggest that qualified graduate librarians across Canada are professional people. They have professional standing. Apparently the government is seeking to deny librarians professional status.
It may be true that the bill refers to a deputy minister. I suggest that simply granting deputy minister status to a librarian does not make him any less a librarian. He is still a librarian. Primarily he is the chief librarian, whether you give him the status of a deputy minister or not. Notwithstanding the arguments that have been advanced, the only method of filling positions of this kind, in order to create an atmosphere of fairness to librarians across Canada, is to fill them with personnel who are fully qualified librarians.
No arguments on the part of the minister are going to get around the arguments that have been put up by the opposition. I suggest it is a very simple matter. There are many hundreds of qualified librarians throughout Canada. For the minister to suggest that there is not in Canada a sufficient group to draw from is an insult to librarians throughout the country.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO IMPLEMENT RECOMMENDATIONS OF JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext: I did not suggest that.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO IMPLEMENT RECOMMENDATIONS OF JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I was unavoidably absent during the first part of this discussion. Will you kindly read the amendment?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO IMPLEMENT RECOMMENDATIONS OF JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext:
It was moved by the hon. member for York-Humber:
That section 1 of the bill be amended by adding the following as subparagraph (4) to the proposed new section 5:
No one shall be eligible to be appointed as parliamentary librarian or associate parliamentary librarian hereunder, unless such person is fully qualified as a librarian holding either the bachelor's or master's degree in library science, of any school or university awarding degrees in library science, recognized by the Canadian library association.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO IMPLEMENT RECOMMENDATIONS OF JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, speaking to that amendment, I find it absurd. I will tell you the reason. I am one of the members of parliament who have used the library to the utmost. All of those who are there, the whole staff, are A-l, perfect. I wonder whether they have any degrees from anywhere. I do not believe in degrees; I believe in efficiency, and they are all efficient. I hope the appointments will be made from people who can compare with those who are in the library of parliament at the present time, and who are in the library of the Supreme Court of Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, to answer a few things that have been said, I must say I became a little confused as the debate went on. Before long the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration was talking back to his colleague the Minister of Fisheries. That really tied me up. First of all, I want to assure the hon. member for Macleod that in this amendment there is certainly no reflection on the present librarians. If there were any reflection in the amendment then the bill itself would be a reflection on the librarians, but everything points to the future, not to the past.
The minister has made much of past appointments by governments to the post of librarian, and pointed out they were not trained librarians. We did not have any library schools or library courses at the universities in those days. It is a comparatively new and struggling profession. I feel the minister has been extremely scornful of librarians as professional people. He read a letter in which it was said that many qualities were needed in a parliamentary librarian, and I would gather insinuated from that letter that probably those qualities could not be found in a trained librarian. This bill, without the amendment, is an insult to all professional librarians across Canada, and that is why we on this side are supporting the amendment.

speechtext: Question.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO IMPLEMENT RECOMMENDATIONS OF JOINT COMMITTEE
speechtext:
No; this is too serious a matter to decide in such a hurry. Let us see what is happening. The Minister of Citizenship and Immigration informed the house that he was bringing the bill before us just as a courteous gesture to carry out the recommendations of the joint committee of both houses. After having made that remarkable statement he went on to make a biased political speech. He could not refrain from that, and he extended it a little later on by casting a slur on Sir John A. Macdonald. He said he made two appointments to the library staff because the library was a joint library, not a parliamentary library. Subsequently in the course of his remarks he said that was done just for political purposes.
That was the type of speech the minister made in introducing the bill, and it was exactly what I expected. He has been doing that all along. He is following the practice of other ministers. He raised the big stick. Immediately the amendment was read he jumped to his feet to say the government was
I Mr. Pouliot.]
opposing it. He said nothing about the joint committee, which had not even considered it. No; the government was opposed to it, and of course when the government is opposed to anything, then we are all supposed to quail and go creeping around. I suppose we should bow three times to the east before we approach this minister.
Not content with that, he then introduced the red herring. This amendment, if passed, would affect the present incumbents of the office. All he had to do was bring in the hydrogen bomb and we would have had the thing complete. He tried to scare us out of our wits.
Then he suggested that the person appointed to the library would be deputy head of the department. No such thing. He may be occupying a position which is recognized as being equivalent to the deputy head of a department, but it is not a department of government. It is just one of those nonsensical arguments put forward with the intention, it seems to me-I hope not, but it appears to be the intention-of misleading the committee. I hope the minister did not have that in mind. However, that is the way in which this bill has been introduced to us. The minister can lay it at his own feet if this measure is delayed.
